title: Raising Believers: A Bible Study for Christian Parents
subtitle: A five-session study on passing a durable faith to children in a secular age.
summary:
This study is for parents, grandparents, and small groups of families who want their children to know God and are quietly afraid that wanting it isn't enough. It moves slowly through five sessions: what the home is for in the forming of faith; teaching the next generation the way the Shema commands, on the road and at the table; answering the hard questions children ask instead of flinching from them; a faith built to survive doubt and the years away from home; and parenting from grace rather than fear. A tired parent can lead it with no preparation. Every question carries a note on what's behind it, and every session ends in prayer rather than a parenting tip.

It won't promise a method that guarantees believing children, and the leader must never let it. Scripture is full of faithful parents whose children walked away; the Bible records sons of godly men who wanted nothing to do with their fathers' God. The home is the main place faith is handed on, and that's true and weighty and worth everything we have. But the home isn't a machine that produces belief, and the gospel, not technique, is finally the hope of any child. The study holds both, and it refuses to sell parents a formula that would leave them crushed and blaming themselves if a child wanders. It starts with its own failures. Most parents have prayed over beds not knowing whether the prayers landed, answered a hard question badly and lain awake about it, and parented from fear and called it diligence. The writer and the leader are among them.
audience: Parents, grandparents, and small groups of families

sessions.title: Whose Work Is This
sessions.aim: To name what the home is for in the forming of a child's faith, neither shrinking from the weight Scripture lays on parents nor turning that weight into a guarantee, and to refuse both the parent who hands discipleship to the church and the parent who believes the right method will save a child.
sessions.summary:
Many parents have done everything right, family devotions, the right school, the right church, and watched a child walk away anyway. They want to know what they did wrong, and they may have done nothing wrong. Somebody told them a child's faith is the sum of a parent's effort. So the first question isn't how to raise a believer. It's whose work this is. One answer says the home is decisive, and it's right that Scripture lays the teaching of children on parents, not programs. Another says only God gives faith, and it's right that the new birth is the Spirit's work, not a curriculum's.

Neither answer gets the whole field. The home isn't the whole cause, which corrects the parent who thinks effort guarantees belief, and it isn't nothing, which corrects the parent who leaves it all to the youth pastor. It's the ordinary ground God most often uses, and also a place where faithful sowing doesn't always bring the harvest a parent prayed for. And Deuteronomy doesn't open with a technique. It opens with "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one" (Deuteronomy 6:4), and with a parent who loves God with everything before teaching anyone.

keyScripture.why: "You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might. And these words that I command you today shall be on your heart. You shall teach them diligently to your children" (Deuteronomy 6:5-7). Before Moses tells parents to teach their children, he tells them to love the Lord. Forming a child's faith is woven into a parent's whole life, not scheduled into a slot.

discussion.q: Before tonight, what did you privately believe a child's faith depended on? The parent's effort, the church's programs, the child's own choice, or God alone?
discussion.behind: Bring the default into the open before defining anything. Most parents carry an unexamined assumption about where the weight falls, and it's usually either crushing or evasive. You're not settling it yet, only exposing the assumption and the fear or comfort attached to it. Go first if the room is slow.

discussion.q: Read Deuteronomy 6:4-9. It doesn't begin with "teach your children." It begins with "love the LORD your God with all your heart." Why do you think the command to the parent comes before the command about the child?
discussion.behind: Move the room off the program reflex. We expect a curriculum and get a call to the parent's own heart first. You can't hand on what you don't have; the teaching flows from a love already alive in the parent. Help them feel the order before they feel the obligation.

discussion.q: The home is the ordinary ground God most often uses, and faithful sowing still doesn't always produce the harvest a parent prayed for. Where have you confused those two, treating the ground as a guarantee?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge of the whole study. Don't let it become a debate about whether parents matter. Keep it on the personal recognition that we slide from "the home matters" to "the home decides," and that the slide sets parents up to be crushed. Getting this right protects everyone who comes after, especially the parent of a prodigal.

discussion.q: One parent says only God gives faith. Another says the home is decisive. What's true in each, and what does each become when it forgets the other?
discussion.behind: Keep the room fair from the start. God alone gives the new heart, and the home is still where he most often works. Make sure no one leaves thinking either that effort is pointless or that effort is everything. The error isn't the truth in each. It's the truth swung as a club, against the lazy parent or against the grieving one.

discussion.q: Many of us have parented from fear and called it diligence. Where have you dressed up your own anxiety about your children as something more respectable?
discussion.behind: Turn the question on ourselves. You're not hunting for a confession to shame anyone. The gospel reaches a fearful parent only after the fear is named, and that includes the leader. Go first.

objections.objection: Faith is caught at home or not at all. If I do family worship faithfully, choose the right schooling, and model a real walk with God, my children will believe. The outcome is in my hands, and a wandering child is proof a parent failed.
objections.response: Half of this is true. Scripture does lay the teaching of children on parents, the home is the ordinary place God hands on faith, and a parent who leaves all of it to a program has missed something Deuteronomy won't let them miss. But look at the record. Isaac raised Esau, who "despised his birthright" (Genesis 25:34). Samuel, who heard God's voice as a boy, had sons who "did not walk in his ways but turned aside after gain" (1 Samuel 8:3). David, a man after God's own heart, watched his sons tear his house apart. If faithful parenting guaranteed believing children, those passages couldn't exist. To tell a grieving parent that a child's unbelief is simply their failure is to claim something Scripture denies, and it's a cruelty that drives broken parents away from the only God who can reach their child. The home matters enormously, but it doesn't control the heart. Only God gives the new heart.

objections.objection: Only God can give faith. Regeneration is entirely the Spirit's work, so all this talk of family worship and answering questions is anxious parents pretending they can do what only God can do. Relax and trust God.
objections.response: Much of this is right. No parent has ever produced a new birth. The new birth is God's work, "not of blood nor of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man, but of God" (John 1:13), and a parent who thinks the right routine manufactures belief has confused himself with the Holy Spirit. That's true, and it's freeing. But the same God who alone gives faith told parents, "You shall teach them diligently to your children" (Deuteronomy 6:7). He ordains means as well as ends, and he works through the ordinary table, the bedtime prayer, and the hard question answered with care. Saying "only God gives faith, so my effort doesn't matter" is like saying "only God gives the harvest, so I won't plant." Trust God, yes, and then sow, because the God you trust told you to.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What's the fear about your child that you've never said out loud, the one you carry into the dark when the house is finally quiet?
sessions.practice: This week, before you try to teach your children anything, tend your own love for God. Each morning, spend five minutes with the Lord you're asking your children to love, not preparing a lesson for them but loving him yourself. Then notice over the week whether what you say to your children about God comes out of that rather than out of fear. Write down what you noticed, and don't judge what you find.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, you gave us these children, and we love them more than we know how to carry. We've treated their faith as something we could secure by being good enough, and we've also, when we were tired, left it to everyone but ourselves. Forgive us both ways. Teach us that you alone give the new heart, and that you've still called us to sow, to teach, and to love you first so our children can see what loving you looks like. Put in us a love for you that they can catch. And the children who have wandered, we put in your hands, because they were always more yours than ours. Amen.
reflection: Where have I treated my child's faith as the sum of my effort, and where have I quietly left it to the church because the weight felt too heavy?
Do I love the Lord first, with my own heart, or am I trying to hand my children a faith I'm not living?
If Deuteronomy puts the parent's love before the child's instruction, where does my own formation need to start?
sessions.teaching:
Think of a father who has done everything right: family devotions every night, a carefully chosen school, a faithful church. His daughter walked away from all of it the moment she could, and he wants to know what he did wrong. He may have done nothing wrong. Somewhere along the way someone taught him that a child's faith is the sum of a parent's effort, so a wandering child can only mean a failed parent. So I don't want to begin with how to raise a believer, which is where every anxious parent wants to begin. I want to begin with a harder question: whose work is this? Until we answer that, every method we reach for will either crush us or let us off the hook.

Two answers want to silence each other, and each deserves to be heard at its strongest. The first says the home is decisive: faith is handed down at the kitchen table, and if you do family worship and model the real thing, your children will believe. It isn't entirely wrong. The Bible lays the teaching of children on parents. Deuteronomy doesn't say drop them at the temple and hope. It says, "these words that I command you today shall be on your heart. You shall teach them diligently to your children" (Deuteronomy 6:6-7). A parent who hands the whole of a child's discipleship to a youth program has missed something Scripture won't let them miss.

The second answer says only God can give faith, that no curriculum produces a new heart, and that our part is only to trust. That isn't wrong either. No parent in history has manufactured a new birth. Faith is a gift, and those who receive Christ are "born, not of blood nor of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man, but of God" (John 1:13). The parent who thinks the right routine guarantees belief has quietly confused himself with God.

Now refuse to let either answer take the whole field. The home isn't the whole cause, and Scripture shows it plainly. Isaac raised Esau. Samuel, who as a boy heard God's voice in the night, had sons who "turned aside after gain. They took bribes and perverted justice" (1 Samuel 8:3). David, the man after God's own heart, cried, "O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! Would I had died instead of you" (2 Samuel 18:33). If faithful parenting controlled the outcome, the Bible couldn't contain those stories. But the home also isn't nothing. The same Scripture that records the prodigals commands the teaching and hands faith down through generations of one family: the God of Abraham, of Isaac, and of Jacob.

So here's where I want us to stand, and the leader has to hold it steady all the way through. The home is the ordinary ground God most often uses to hand on faith, the most important human soil there is. And the home isn't a machine that produces belief, because faithful sowing doesn't always yield the harvest a parent prayed for, and a child's heart finally belongs to God. Some of you need to stop leaving your children's faith to everyone but you. Some of you need to put down a weight you were never strong enough to carry, the belief that your child's soul is yours to secure. Many of you need both.

I have five sons, and I can't save a single one of them. No parent escapes this. Most of us have parented from fear and called it diligence, prayed over beds not knowing whether a word landed, and answered a hard question badly and lain awake replaying it as if our mistake could cost a soul.

Then notice how Deuteronomy begins, because it changes everything. It doesn't open with a technique. It opens with "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one. You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might" (Deuteronomy 6:4-5). The command to the parent comes before the command about the child. You can't hand on what you don't hold. The teaching of children begins with a parent whose own heart loves the Lord, and who then, out of the overflow, talks about him at home and on the road, lying down and rising up. That's mercy, and it's where we go next.

scriptureStudy.note: "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one. You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart." The command to the parent comes first. Before any instruction about children, the parent is told to love God wholly, because that love is what's being handed down.

"These words that I command you today shall be on your heart. You shall teach them diligently to your children." The teaching flows outward from the parent's heart, and it's constant rather than scheduled, woven into the road and the table and the falling asleep and the waking.

"Isaac loved Esau because he ate of his game, but Rebekah loved Jacob." A household in the line of promise was divided, and a son raised in it despised his birthright (25:34). Even faithful homes don't control every child's heart.
"Yet his sons did not walk in his ways but turned aside after gain." The boy who heard God in the night raised sons who took bribes. Godly parenting doesn't guarantee godly children.
"O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! Would I had died instead of you." David, a man after God's own heart, grieves a rebel son. A faithful parent can still weep over a wandering child.

"Train up a child in the way he should go; even when he is old he will not depart from it." A proverb states how things generally go, not an iron promise. Read as a guarantee, it has crushed many faithful parents whose child wandered.

"He gave the right to become children of God, who were born, not of blood nor of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man, but of God." The new birth is God's work, not the parent's, which humbles our pride and frees us from a weight we were never meant to carry.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, look at the long argument the church has had about how faith passes between generations, because today's parent inherits both a great confidence and a great anxiety. For much of Christian history the household was assumed to be where faith was learned: catechism at the table, prayers at night, belief passed down like any other family inheritance. There was real truth in that. Faith is more apprenticed than argued, learned by living near someone who lives it. But that confidence could harden into the assumption that a child raised in a believing household would simply believe, which the Bible's own record of rebellious sons refutes.

Set that beside the modern picture, in which the home has been steadily emptied of its forming weight. Faith gets handed to an hour of programming a week, the parent becomes a driver to youth group, and the wider culture teaches every child that belief is a private preference to be chosen later, if at all. Weigh both errors. Keep from the older tradition its conviction that the home is the primary soil, where faith is handed on by nearness rather than by professionals. And keep the insight that the new heart is God's gift, which no household can manufacture. Parents are commanded to sow with everything they have, and forbidden to claim the harvest as their own achievement.

memoryVerse.text: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might.

sessions.title: On the Road and at the Table
sessions.aim: To take seriously what the Shema tells parents to do, to talk of God's words constantly in the ordinary rhythms of a shared life, and to see family worship not as a performance to dread but as the everyday repetition by which a child learns whose they are.
sessions.summary:
Moses gives Scripture's most direct instruction for passing faith to children, and it isn't what we expect. He doesn't say enroll them, schedule them, or out-argue their doubts. He says talk: "when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise" (Deuteronomy 6:7). Why would God lay so much on dinner-table conversation and bedtime words? The skeptic says it's naive. Plenty of children heard Bible talk every day and walked away, and constant religious words can produce resentment as easily as faith.

That deserves weight. The talk isn't magic. But the instruction isn't "say enough words and the child will believe." It's "let the faith fill the ordinary," so a child grows up in a home where God isn't a Sunday topic but part of how the family lives. And the talk comes after the command to love God, so it's meant to be the overflow of a real love, not a substitute for one. What forms a child isn't a flawless devotional but a faith made normal and a parent's own dependence on God.

keyScripture.why: "You shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise" (Deuteronomy 6:7). Forming faith happens in the ordinary rhythms of a shared life, the whole of an ordinary day, rather than in a scheduled program.

discussion.q: Moses says to talk of these words at home, on the road, lying down, and rising up. What's your gut reaction to how ordinary and constant that is, and what does the reaction show you?
discussion.behind: Get the gut response before the Bible study. Many will feel they fall short, or that it sounds exhausting, and that's worth examining. We'd often rather have a tidy slot than a life with God woven through it.

discussion.q: Plenty of children heard Bible talk every day and walked away, some resenting it. What's true in that objection, and what does it miss about what the Shema is after?
discussion.behind: Keep both halves. Words alone guarantee nothing and can breed resentment when they ring hollow. But the Shema isn't after a volume of words; it's after a faith made normal and lived, flowing from a parent who loves God. Help the room hear the difference between nagging and a home where faith is simply part of life.

discussion.q: Where in your home has faith become a scheduled topic rather than part of the ordinary air? What might change it?
discussion.behind: This is the quiet, practical center. Many of us have fenced God into a devotional slot and a Sunday. Press on the difference between God as a subject and God as the atmosphere, and let people imagine him woven back into ordinary life.

discussion.q: The family worship that forms children isn't the flawless one but the ordinary, repeated one. Does that relieve you, or does the phrase "family worship" still intimidate you? Why?
discussion.behind: Let people admit the dread. Many carry guilt and a picture of an ideal devotional they can never sustain. What forms a child is consistency and reality, not polish, and a short, imperfect practice kept up beats a grand one abandoned.

discussion.q: Looking back, what did your own childhood teach you about whether God belonged in the ordinary parts of life? How is that shaping the home you're building now?
discussion.behind: Close by turning to ourselves. Many of us keep faith tidy and scheduled because a life with God woven through it feels too exposing. Invite people to name what they inherited and what they want to hand on differently. Go first. The point is reflection, not resolution.

objections.objection: This is naive. Plenty of kids heard Bible verses at every meal and prayers at every bedtime and walked away the second they left home. Constant religious talk doesn't produce faith. It produces resentment.
objections.response: There's real weight in this. Many children raised on a steady diet of religious words left, and some left precisely because the words were everywhere and the reality was nowhere, because the talk was nagging rather than love, and God was a rule enforced rather than a person enjoyed. That kind of home breeds exactly the resentment the objection names. But look at what the Shema is after. It isn't "say enough words and the child will believe." The command to talk constantly comes right after the command for the parent to love the Lord with all the heart, so the talk is meant to be the overflow of a real love, not a replacement for it. A child can tell the difference between a parent for whom God is the air they breathe and a parent for whom God is a topic to enforce. The first fills a home; the second only nags. The Shema asks for the first. It's no guarantee, but it's a very different thing from the resentment the objection rightly fears.

objections.objection: If I just have family devotions every day, won't that be enough? I can commit to a routine. Give me the program and I'll run it, and my children will turn out fine.
objections.response: Slow down, because that eagerness hides the very error this study resists. Daily family worship is good, and you should do it, and consistency matters more than polish. But the Shema won't give you a program with a guaranteed outcome. It describes a life full of God, of which a daily devotional is one good part, and it places that life downstream of a parent who loves God. A routine run as a box to check, with a heart that's elsewhere, teaches a child that faith is a performance to get through. The aim isn't to run a program well enough to secure a result. It's to live near God, in front of your children, every ordinary day, and leave the result to him. Do the family worship. Just don't mistake the doing for the having, or the routine for a guarantee.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If your children grow up and describe what your home taught them about God, what are you afraid they'd say, and what do you long for them to say?
sessions.practice: This week, do what the Shema says in one small way. Pick an ordinary moment you already share with your children, the drive to school, a meal, the minutes before sleep, and bring God into it naturally, not as a lecture but as a real word from your own life with him. Tell them one true thing God has done in you, or ask them one real question and listen. Do it every day. Write down whether faith felt a little more like the air of your home by the end of the week.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, you didn't ask us to schedule you into our children's lives. You asked us to live so near you that you spill into the road and the table and the dark before sleep. Forgive us for fencing you into a slot, and forgive us for the times our talk about you was nagging and not love. Make our love for you real enough that our children catch it, not because we said the right words but because they grew up breathing the air we breathe. Be the atmosphere of our homes. And by your Spirit, give faith to the children we're raising in them. Amen.
reflection: Has God become a scheduled topic in my home or the ordinary air my children breathe, and what would it take to move from the first to the second?
Where has my talk about God been nagging rather than the overflow of real love, and what does that show about my own walk?
What ordinary moment in our family's week could I bring God into this week without making it a lecture?
sessions.teaching:
Moses gives the most direct instruction in Scripture for how faith passes to the next generation, and it's almost embarrassingly ordinary. He doesn't say enroll your children in the right institution, schedule them into the right programs, or arm yourself to out-argue their future doubts. He says talk about these words. "You shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise" (Deuteronomy 6:7). Why would God put so much weight on dinner conversation and bedtime words? If we don't understand the method, we'll either dismiss it as too little or turn it into a grim program, and it's neither.

Start with the skeptic, because his objection is fair. This is naive, he says, and he points to the children who heard Bible verses at every meal and prayers at every bedtime and walked away the moment they were free, some of them because of the words, tired of a faith that was always talked about and never apparently lived. That's true. Constant religious talk can produce resentment as readily as faith, and a home where God is a rule enforced and a topic nagged often breeds exactly the rebellion the skeptic describes. The talk isn't magic.

But the skeptic has misread the Shema. The command to talk doesn't stand alone. It comes right after "You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might," and right after "these words... shall be on your heart" (Deuteronomy 6:5-6). The order is everything. The talk is meant to be the overflow of a full heart, not a substitute for an empty one, and children can tell the difference. A child knows, with a discernment that puts adults to shame, whether God is the air a parent breathes or a subject a parent enforces. When God is the air, the talk on the road and at the table isn't nagging. It's the natural spilling over of a life turned toward him, the way a family that loves music has music all over the house without anyone scheduling it. When God is only a subject, the same words land as pressure.

So the Shema doesn't ask for a volume of religious words. It asks for a faith so normal, so woven into the ordinary, that a child grows up unable to remember a time when God wasn't part of how the family lived and talked and made decisions and went to sleep. Israel's worship was built this way. At Passover, "when your children say to you, 'What do you mean by this service?' you shall say, 'It is the sacrifice of the LORD's Passover'" (Exodus 12:26-27). The meal was meant to make children ask. And the psalmist says, "We will not hide them from their children, but tell to the coming generation the glorious deeds of the LORD... so that they should set their hope in God" (Psalm 78:4, 7).

Here a word about family worship, because the phrase makes faithful parents flinch with guilt. They picture a flawless devotional with every child rapt and no one squirming, a scene that has never happened in any home. The family worship that forms children isn't the flawless one. It's the ordinary, repeated, often interrupted one: a short reading and a clumsy prayer, done again tomorrow and the day after, for years. Consistency forms a child far more than polish. A simple practice kept up beats a grand one abandoned in shame after two weeks. Timothy knew the Scriptures "from childhood" (2 Timothy 3:15), and his faith "dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice" (2 Timothy 1:5). That's what ordinary repetition in a believing home looks like.

The repetition doesn't cause the new heart. Only God gives that. But it's the furniture of a home in which, if God gives faith, the child will already know its language and the love it rests in, with the words of the faith in their bones and the memory of a parent leaning on God.

And we have to admit our own instinct here, because for many of us it runs the other way. We'd rather keep faith tidy and scheduled, in a box we can control, because a life with God woven through it is exposing. It means our children see our actual dependence on God, or the lack of it, in how we handle bad news and late bills. The Shema won't let us keep God in a box, because a God in a box isn't the air, and the air is what forms a child. So bring God into the ordinary, not as a program to run but as a life to live in front of them. Do the family worship, simply and imperfectly, every day you can. Talk about him the way you talk about everything else that's real to you. Then leave the result, the new heart you can't give, with the One who can.

scriptureStudy.note: "Talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise." The four phrases cover a whole ordinary day, which is the point. Faith isn't a slot in the day but the atmosphere of all of it.

"When your son asks you in time to come... then you shall say to your son, 'We were Pharaoh's slaves in Egypt. And the LORD brought us out.'" Faith is handed on as story and testimony, a rescue retold, not a list of rules enforced.

"Tell to the coming generation the glorious deeds of the LORD... so that they should set their hope in God." The telling is deliberate and spans generations, aimed not at information but at hope set on God.
"One generation shall commend your works to another, and shall declare your mighty acts." Faith passes down as one generation telling the next what God has done.

"When your children say to you, 'What do you mean by this service?' you shall say, 'It is the sacrifice of the LORD's Passover.'" God built children's questions into the rhythm of worship, expecting the meal to make them ask.

"A faith that dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice and now, I am sure, dwells in you as well." Paul traces Timothy's faith through two generations of women, belief handed on through a faithful home.
"Knowing from whom you learned it and how from childhood you have been acquainted with the sacred writings." Timothy knew the Scriptures from childhood, the very immersion the Shema describes.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, think about the difference between formation and information, because the Shema describes the first and the modern home keeps reaching for the second. Older traditions understood that belief is more apprenticed than taught. A child learns to pray the way a child learns a mother tongue, by immersion long before understanding, by living in a home where the practices are simply done and the language simply spoken until it becomes the child's own. Table grace, bedtime prayer, a weekly rhythm of rest and worship, the sight of a parent on their knees: these formed children less by transferring facts than by shaping loves and habits and a sense of the world as a place where God is real and near. James K. A. Smith develops a similar argument in You Are What You Love (2016), that we're formed less by what we think than by what we love, and that loves are shaped by practice.

Set this beside the modern instinct to treat faith as information, propositions explained well enough that a child will agree, an instinct sharpened by a culture that frames belief as a private opinion chosen after weighing evidence. Weigh both: information matters. Children need to know what they believe and why, and a faith with no content collapses under the first hard question. But information without formation produces a child who can pass a doctrine quiz with no love for God. The discipline the Shema asks for is to recover formation without neglecting the content that love will one day need to defend.
