sessions.title: When They Ask the Hard Things
sessions.aim: To welcome a child's hard questions as something Scripture expects rather than a threat to fear, and to learn to answer them truthfully, including the ones we can't answer, so that home becomes a safe place to doubt out loud.
sessions.summary:
Children ask hard things, and they always have. Passover itself was built around a child's question: "What do you mean by this service?" (Exodus 12:26). So the first question for parents isn't how to have all the answers. It's what to do with the questions we can't answer, about suffering and hell and science and the silence of God. The strong form of the fear says that admitting you don't know will shake a child's faith, that a parent must project certainty or the whole structure wobbles. There's something to that. A child needs to know the ground is solid.

But the fear is wrong about what makes ground solid. A parent who fakes certainty, shuts a question down, or answers a real doubt with a slogan teaches a child two things: that the question is dangerous, and that the parent can't be trusted with it. So the next doubt goes elsewhere or gets buried. The home that raises a durable faith isn't the home with all the answers. It's the home where any question is safe, where "I don't know" is said plainly and then we look together, so that when the real storms come, the child comes home with them instead of going away.

keyScripture.why: "When your son asks you in time to come, 'What is the meaning of the testimonies and the statutes and the rules that the LORD our God has commanded you?' then you shall say to your son, 'We were Pharaoh's slaves in Egypt. And the LORD brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand'" (Deuteronomy 6:20-21). God built the child's question into the faith, and gave the parent not a slogan but a story to answer it with.

discussion.q: What's a hard question one of your children has asked, or that you dread them asking, that you didn't feel ready for? How did you respond, or how do you imagine responding?
discussion.behind: Start with the real and specific. Most parents carry one particular dreaded question. Bring it into the open, and make it normal that children ask hard things and parents feel unready, so no one feels alone in the fear. Go first with one of your own.

discussion.q: Many parents fear that admitting they don't know will shake a child's faith. What's true in that worry, and how is it wrong about what makes a child's faith solid?
discussion.behind: Keep both halves: children do need solid ground, but faked certainty doesn't provide it. Help the room see that candor about the limits of your knowledge, joined to confidence in God, is sturdier than a pretense that can't survive the first real challenge.

discussion.q: A parent who shuts down a hard question teaches a child that the question is dangerous and that the parent can't be trusted with it. Have you seen that happen, in your own childhood or your own home?
discussion.behind: This can be tender, because some in the room were shut down as children and some have shut down their own kids. Go gently. The goal is to be trusted with the hard things, not to have all the answers.

discussion.q: Read Matthew 11:2-6. John the Baptist, in prison, sends to ask Jesus, "Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?" How does Jesus answer the doubt? What does that suggest about treating doubt as part of faith rather than its enemy?
discussion.behind: Let people push back, because some traditions taught that doubt is sin, and the leader mustn't steamroll that. But Scripture is full of hard questions brought to God, in the Psalms, in Job, and here, and Jesus answers John with evidence, not a rebuke. A faith never allowed to ask is a faith that breaks quietly.

discussion.q: Where have you reached for a slogan because the true answer felt too risky? What were you afraid of?
discussion.behind: Close by turning to ourselves. We reach for pat answers out of our own fear, not the child's good. Go first. The point isn't guilt but seeing that our slogans usually protect us rather than them, and that children can tell.

objections.objection: If I admit to my child that I don't know something about God, I'll shake their faith. Children need a parent who is certain. The moment I show doubt, the whole structure wobbles and they lose confidence in everything.
objections.response: There's a real truth under this. A child does need to feel the ground is solid, needs parents who aren't blown about by every wind, and draws security from a parent's settled confidence. But the fear assumes that faked certainty is what makes the ground solid, and a pretended certainty is the most fragile thing in the house. It shatters the moment a child meets a question the parent can't bluff past, and then the child concludes the whole faith was a bluff. Real solidity is a parent who can say, "I don't know that one. It's a hard question, and a lot of people who love God have wrestled with it. Let's look at it together," while staying unshaken in their confidence in the God they do know. That child learns that faith is strong enough to hold a question, that doubt isn't a threat, and that their parent is truthful and can be trusted with the next question too. What a child needs is confidence in God, not a parent pretending to know everything.

objections.objection: I'm not a theologian. I can't answer questions about evolution and the problem of evil and the canon of Scripture. Shouldn't I just hand my children to the experts, the apologists and youth pastors, and stay out of it?
objections.response: No, and there's real relief here, because the question assumes you have to be an expert, and you don't. Deuteronomy doesn't arm parents with a philosophy. It hands them a story: when your child asks what this means, tell him, "We were Pharaoh's slaves in Egypt. And the LORD brought us out." You answer a hard question first with testimony, with what God has actually done, including in your own life, which no expert can give your child and you can. For the hard intellectual questions, your job isn't to have memorized the answer but to be the trusted person who takes the question seriously and goes looking with them. "I don't fully know; let's find out together" is a faithful answer, and the looking together teaches more than a slick answer would. Use the experts as help, good books and wiser friends, but don't hand over the relationship. The point was never that you'd win every argument. It was that you'd be the safe place your child brings the question, and that can't be outsourced.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What question about God have you never resolved for yourself, the doubt you carry quietly, and how does it shape the way you respond when your child asks something hard?
sessions.practice: This week, make your home safer for hard questions on purpose. In an ordinary, unpressured moment, ask one of your children, "What's something about God or the Bible that doesn't make sense to you, or that you wonder about?" Whatever they say, don't correct it, fix it, or panic. Receive it and thank them for asking. If you don't know, say so, and offer to look into it together. Write down what they asked and what it cost you not to reach for a slogan.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, our children will ask the things we're afraid of, about suffering and silence and whether you're even there, and we've been so afraid of the questions that we've sometimes made our homes unsafe for them. Forgive us for the slogans we reached for to protect ourselves. Make us truthful enough to say we don't know, and confident enough in you to say it without fear. Let our homes be the place our children bring their hardest doubts, so that when the storms come they come toward us and toward you, and not away. You can hold every question they'll ever ask. Help us trust that. Amen.
reflection: When my child asks something hard, whose comfort am I protecting with my answer, theirs or mine, and what am I afraid of?
Is my home a place where a doubt can be said out loud and met with candor, or a place where questions are quietly understood to be dangerous?
What hard question have I been avoiding, and what would it look like to look for the answer with my child rather than pretend I already have it?
sessions.teaching:
Children ask hard things, and they always have, and God knew they would. Look at how Passover was built: "And when your children say to you, 'What do you mean by this service?' you shall say, 'It is the sacrifice of the LORD's Passover'" (Exodus 12:26-27). The question isn't an interruption of worship. It's designed into it. God ordained a meal strange enough that a child would have to ask, and then he told the parents what to say. So before we're afraid of our children's questions, notice that the God who made our children expects them and isn't threatened by a single one. The fear is ours, not his.

The first real question for us isn't how to have all the answers, because we won't. It's what to do with the questions we can't answer: why good people suffer, why God seems silent, how faith fits with what they're learning in science class, whether any of it is true. Those questions are coming, and a secular culture presses them harder and earlier than it pressed them on us.

The fear most of us feel goes like this. If I admit I don't know, I'll shake my child's faith. Children need a parent who's certain, and the moment I show a crack the whole structure wobbles. There's truth buried in that. A child needs to feel the ground under them is solid and draws security from parents who aren't tossed about by every wind. But the fear has the wrong idea of what solid ground is. A pretended, I-have-all-the-answers certainty is the most fragile thing in the house, because it depends on the parent never being caught not knowing. The parent will be caught. And the day a child realizes the certainty was a bluff is the day the child quietly concludes the whole faith was a bluff.

Real solidity is a parent who can say, "I don't know the answer to that one. It's a hard question, and people who love God deeply have wrestled with it for centuries. Let's look at it together," while staying unshaken in confidence in the God they do know. Watch what that child learns. The faith is sturdy enough to hold a hard question. Doubt isn't something to hide. And their parent is truthful, which means their parent is safe, which means the next question, and the terrible one that comes at nineteen, will come home rather than be carried off somewhere else or buried.

A parent who shuts a question down teaches two things. The question is dangerous, a threat to faith rather than part of it. And the parent can't be trusted with it. A child who learns those two things doesn't stop having doubts. They stop bringing them to you. They take them to the internet, to a skeptical friend, to a professor glad to receive them, or they bury them until the faith collapses from the inside with no one knowing it was hollow.

Scripture isn't afraid of the questions, and that should free us. The Psalms are full of "How long, O LORD?" (Psalm 13:1). Job spends chapter after chapter demanding an answer from God, and God's anger falls at the end on the friends, not on Job. John the Baptist, in prison, sent to ask Jesus, "Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?" (Matthew 11:3). Jesus didn't call it unbelief. He sent back evidence: the blind see, the lame walk, the poor have good news preached to them. A desperate father cried, "I believe; help my unbelief!" (Mark 9:24), and Jesus healed his son. Doubt brought to God isn't faith's enemy. It's often the road faith travels to become real.

Most of us have to admit we've failed at this. We've answered a child's hard question with a slogan that shut the conversation down, and lain awake afterward knowing why. We did it to protect ourselves. The true answer felt too exposing of how much we haven't figured out, so we reached for the slogan, and the child could tell, the way children always can, that we'd closed a door instead of opening one.

So here's the aim, and it's a freeing one. The home that raises a durable faith isn't the home with all the answers. No home has those. It's the home where any question is safe, where "I don't know" is said without panic, and where doubt is met with "let's look at this together" rather than a wall. You don't have to be a theologian. Deuteronomy didn't hand parents a philosophy. It handed them a story, what God has done, told truthfully, including what he's done in you. Peter tells believers to be "always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and respect" (1 Peter 3:15), and with a child the gentleness and respect matter as much as the reasons. Be the safe place. Welcome the questions God himself built into your children, and trust that the God who isn't threatened by any of them can hold every doubt your child will ever bring.

scriptureStudy.note: "When your children say to you, 'What do you mean by this service?' you shall say, 'It is the sacrifice of the LORD's Passover.'" God designed worship to prompt a child's question, so the question isn't a threat to faith but a doorway into it.

"Then you shall say to your son, 'We were Pharaoh's slaves in Egypt. And the LORD brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand.'" A parent answers first with testimony, what God has actually done, which no outside expert can give a child.
"How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever?" Scripture models anguished questioning of God, which tells us doubt brought to God isn't outside the life of faith but woven through it.

"Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind and said: 'Who is this that darkens counsel by words without knowledge? Dress for action like a man; I will question you, and you make it known to me.'" God answers Job's questions not by rebuking him for asking but with his own presence.
"Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?" Even John the Baptist doubted, and Jesus met the doubt with evidence rather than condemnation.
"I believe; help my unbelief!" The father holds faith and doubt in one breath, and Jesus answers by healing his son. Faith is often faith still wrestling.

"Always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and respect." Be ready with reasons, and the manner, gentleness and respect, is as much the instruction as the readiness.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, look at what research on young adults and faith has found, because it's close to the opposite of what an anxious parent expects. Kara Powell and Chap Clark's Sticky Faith (2011), drawing on research at Fuller Youth Institute, reported that young people whose faith lasted into adulthood were often not the ones from homes that suppressed doubt, but ones who'd had room to voice their hardest questions inside warm relationships before they left home. Doubt engaged in a safe place tended to go with lasting faith. Doubt forbidden and driven underground tended to go with a faith that looked fine until it gave way, often in the first year away. The same research warned that a faith reduced to behavior management, rules with God attached and the gospel missing, didn't hold, because there was nothing in it worth keeping once the rules no longer applied.

Don't turn this into one more technique. The deepest finding is a posture, not a program: warmth, candor, and a home safe for doubt are the soil in which faith more often survives, while pretense, suppression, and rule-bound moralism are the soil in which it more often dies. Research promises outcomes no more than Scripture does, and faithful parents who did everything the studies commend have still watched children leave. But it confirms the shape of wisdom. The goal isn't to win the arguments but to be the trusted place the questions come home to, and to hold up not a list of rules but the gospel itself.

sessions.title: A Faith That Survives Leaving
sessions.aim: To prepare children not for a sheltered faith that has never been tested but for a faith that can stand in a world that doesn't believe, by building convictions deep enough to survive doubt, distance, and the years away from home.
sessions.summary:
The day comes when a child leaves, for college or work or simply adulthood, and walks into a world that assumes their faith is naive and offers them a whole community for leaving it. What kind of faith survives that? The protective instinct says keep them away from the doubts, the dangerous books, the skeptical friends, the hard professors: build the walls high enough. There's love in that, and some sheltering of the young is simply wisdom. But as the whole strategy, it produces the brittle faith it fears, a hothouse faith that has never met a real objection and dies in the first frost.

The faith that survives leaving isn't the one protected from every challenge. It's the one given roots: it knows not only what it believes but why; it met its first hard questions at home with a parent rather than alone at nineteen with a stranger eager to take it apart; and it rests on a real relationship with God, not only the rules and warmth of a believing household. Paul's word is "rooted and built up in him and established in the faith" (Colossians 2:7). You can't fireproof a child. You can send them out with roots deep enough to find water in a dry place, and then entrust them to the One who holds them when they're beyond your reach.

keyScripture.why: "Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord" (Ephesians 6:4). Paul joins a warning against the harshness that drives children away to a call to real formation in the Lord, the roots a child needs to stand when they finally leave.

discussion.q: When you picture your child leaving home and entering a world that doesn't share their faith, what's your honest fear, and what's your instinct for preventing it?
discussion.behind: Start with the fear and the instinct together, because the instinct is usually to protect by sheltering. Name the fear plainly and bring the protective reflex into view, so the room can then ask whether it produces what it wants.

discussion.q: Read Matthew 13:3-9 and 18-23. The seed on rocky ground "has no root in himself," and when trouble comes it falls away. How have you seen that happen to a faith that looked alive? Does it ring true, or do you want to resist it?
discussion.behind: Keep both halves. The protective instinct is love, and the leader should honor it. But sheltering alone can produce a faith never tested and so not trusted by the person who holds it. Let people push back, and help them feel the difference between protecting and isolating.

discussion.q: There's a difference between a faith that knows what it believes and a faith that knows why. Which did you leave home with, and what difference did it make when your faith was first challenged?
discussion.behind: Make it personal. Many in the room left home with one or the other and remember what happened at the first real challenge. Roots, the why under the what, are what let a faith find water when the surface dries out.

discussion.q: Is it better for a child to meet their first hard doubts at home with a parent than alone at nineteen with a stranger eager to take their faith apart? How does that change the way you think about the questions you've been afraid to let your child ask?
discussion.behind: Tie this back to session three and forward to letting go. Engaging doubt early at home isn't a risk to faith but the preparation for leaving. Help parents see the dreaded questions as rehearsal for the storms ahead.

discussion.q: Where are you tempted to shelter rather than to root, and why?
discussion.behind: Close by turning to ourselves. The sheltering instinct is strong, and the leader shares it. We reach for walls because rooting is slower and harder and feels less safe. Go first. The point is to move from protecting to preparing.

objections.objection: The way to keep my children believing is to protect them. Keep them in the right schools, away from the dangerous books and skeptical friends and godless professors. Build the walls high enough, and their faith will be safe.
objections.response: There's love under this, the proper instinct of a parent to guard a child from harm, and some sheltering of the young is right and good; a six-year-old doesn't need to debate atheists. But taken alone, the instinct works against itself. A faith that has only ever been protected, that has never met a real objection, has never been tested, and a child can't fully trust an untested faith when the test comes, and it comes for everyone. The walls don't hold forever. The day arrives when the child leaves the protected world and meets, all at once and without you, every question you kept out, often from people who are skilled at taking faith apart and glad to do it. The hothouse plant dies in the first frost. The answer isn't no protection. It's protection that gives way, over the growing years, to preparation, so a child meets the hard things gradually and with you, while the meeting is still survivable.

objections.objection: If my child walks away from the faith after I've done everything right, it means I failed and the whole effort was pointless. Why pour myself into rooting their faith if there's no guarantee it will hold?
objections.response: Hold this one gently, because it's the deepest fear under the whole session. First, the premise is wrong. A wandering child doesn't prove a failed parent; Isaac, Samuel, and David all watched children turn away. Faithfulness in a parent and faith in a child aren't the same thing, and only God gives the second. Second, you root a child's faith for the same reason a farmer plants in ground he can't control: you're commanded to sow, and the harvest belongs to God. The effort isn't pointless because the outcome is uncertain, any more than prayer is pointless because God is sovereign. And there's a quiet comfort in the parable of the prodigal. The son in the far country "came to himself" and remembered his father's house (Luke 15:17). The rooting goes with a child where you can't, into the hands of a God who can reach them there. You aren't guaranteed the harvest, and you aren't the one who gives it, but the rooting isn't wasted.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If your child is going to face the hardest challenges to their faith without you in the room, what's the one thing you most want to have put deep in them before they go?
sessions.practice: This week, do one thing to root rather than merely shelter. Pick a belief your child holds and gently ask why they believe it, not to test them but to help them find the reasons under the assumption. If they don't have a reason, explore one together. With an older child, consider meeting a real objection together, so the first encounter happens at your table and not alone later. Write down what you learned about the depth, or thinness, of their roots.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, the day is coming when our children will walk out of our protection into a world that will press them hard, and we're afraid. We've wanted to build the walls high and keep the cold out, and we're learning that the walls don't finally hold. Teach us to root them instead, to give them not only what to believe but why, and to let them meet hard things with us while we're still here, so they aren't alone when the storms come. And for the day they're beyond our reach, we entrust them to you, who hold them where we can't and can find a wandering child in any far country. Be their root and their water. Amen.
reflection: Am I building walls to keep the hard world out, or roots that will let my child's faith find water in a dry place, and what is the difference costing me?
Does my child know not only what they believe but why, and where are their roots thinnest right now?
What am I afraid would happen if I let my child meet a real objection while still at home with me, and is that fear protecting them or me?
sessions.teaching:
The day comes for every parent when a child walks out of the home you built into a world that doesn't believe what you taught them. That world quietly assumes their faith is naive, offers them whole communities of people who have left it and are glad they did, and presses on them, all at once and far from your kitchen table, every hard question you may have spent eighteen years keeping at bay. So what kind of faith survives that? A faith that has only ever been sheltered very often doesn't.

The protective instinct is the strongest one most of us have as parents, and it deserves respect. It says the way to keep your children believing is to keep them safe: the right schools, the dangerous books off the shelf, the skeptical friends at a distance, the walls of the home high and thick enough that doubts can't get in. There's real love in that, the love of a parent who'd put their own body between a child and harm. And some sheltering of the young isn't just right but required. A six-year-old doesn't need the problem of evil handed to her. A ten-year-old doesn't need to debate atheists. Age-appropriate protection is simply wisdom.

But watch what happens when sheltering is the whole strategy, all the way to the door. A faith that has only ever been protected has never been tested, and a child can't fully trust an untested faith when the test arrives, because it arrives for everyone. The walls were never built to hold forever. One day the child steps outside them, and on the other side is every question you kept out, often presented by people who are intelligent and articulate and pleased to take a sheltered faith apart. Jesus described this. The seed on rocky ground "immediately receives it with joy, yet he has no root in himself, but endures for a while, and when tribulation or persecution arises on account of the word, immediately he falls away" (Matthew 13:20-21). The faith kept too safe becomes the faith least able to survive.

The faith that survives leaving is the faith that was given roots. "Therefore, as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him, rooted and built up in him and established in the faith" (Colossians 2:6-7). The difference between a sheltered faith and a rooted one is the difference between a child who knows what they believe and a child who knows why. A faith that's only a list is fine until someone challenges the list, and then there's nothing underneath. A rooted faith has the reasons and the relationship and the experience of God beneath the surface, and roots let a plant find water when the ground dries out. Jeremiah's picture is of a tree "planted by water, that sends out its roots by the stream, and does not fear when heat comes" (Jeremiah 17:8).

Here's the practical wisdom that ties the study together. It's far better for a child to meet their first hard doubt at home, at thirteen or fifteen, with a parent beside them who loves them and loves God and isn't afraid of the question, than to meet it for the first time at nineteen, alone in a dorm room, with a brilliant stranger across the hall who has been waiting for exactly that conversation. The doubts are coming either way. What you can shape is whether the first encounter happens at home, as a rehearsal, with you, or later and alone. That's why the questions of session three aren't a threat to faith but preparation for leaving. Every hard question welcomed at your table is a small, survivable exposure that builds strength to meet the real thing standing up.

For most of us the instinct still runs toward the walls. We want to keep the cold world and its clever objections away from our children, and we have to learn, slowly and against everything in us, that the walls don't finally hold, and that the most loving thing is to give them roots deep enough to stand in a hard climate and to let them feel a little of the cold while we're still there to stand in it with them.

And here's the last and hardest truth. You can't fireproof a child. No depth of roots and no perfection of preparation guarantees that a faith will hold, because a child's heart belongs to God, and faithful parents have sent deeply rooted children into the world and watched them wander anyway. The aim was never a guarantee. It's to send them out with roots deep enough to find water in a dry place, having met the hard things with you before they had to meet them alone. And then to do the thing that's harder than all the rooting and sheltering together, which is to let them go and entrust them to the One who holds them when they've walked past the edge of everything you can reach.

scriptureStudy.note: "Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord." Warning and command sit together. Harshness that embitters drives children away; real formation in the Lord gives them roots to stand.

"Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right. 'Honor your father and mother.'" Honoring parents is learned at home, where a child first practices living under an authority beyond themselves.

"As you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him, rooted and built up in him and established in the faith." The image is the root, a faith established deep enough to hold, which is what a child leaving home most needs.

"He is like a tree planted by water, that sends out its roots by the stream, and does not fear when heat comes." The rooted tree isn't afraid of the dry season, because its roots reach the water below.

"He has no root in himself, but endures for a while, and when tribulation or persecution arises on account of the word, immediately he falls away." Jesus names rootlessness as the reason a faith that looked alive collapses under the first real heat.
"The younger son gathered all he had... and there he squandered his property in reckless living." Even in the far country, the son still remembers his father's house (15:17).

"But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him." The father doesn't chase his son into the far country. He watches, and runs toward the one who returns, a picture of entrusting a child to God.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, think about what a secular culture does to a young believer, because the challenge isn't only a set of arguments but a whole environment that makes belief feel implausible. The philosopher Charles Taylor, in A Secular Age (2007), argued that the modern change is less about new arguments against God than about a shift in the conditions of belief: faith, once the assumed background, has become one option among many, and a contested one, surrounded by other ways of living that seem just as reasonable and far easier. A young adult leaving home rarely loses faith to a knockdown argument. More often it's a hundred small pressures: no one nearby who believes, the social cost of standing out, the plausibility of unbelief in a setting built without God, practices quietly dropped, and the discovery that you can stop and nothing visible happens.

Set this beside the research from session three, which found that young people who held on were often part of a real community, kept practices that survived the move, had thought through their faith rather than only inheriting it, and had a relationship with God that was their own. If the challenge is an environment and not only an argument, then roots means more than apologetics. It means a faith practiced and owned, woven into the child's own life and not only the family's, connected to a wider church they can find again after they leave, and centered on a personal trust in God rather than the borrowed warmth of home.

memoryVerse.text: Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.

sessions.title: Grace, Not Fear, and the Letting Go
sessions.aim: To bring the study to the truth under all the others, that we don't finally save our children by parenting them well but entrust them to the God who saves, and to free parents from parenting out of fear into parenting out of grace.
sessions.summary:
Every other session ends with something for the parent to do: love God first, talk about him constantly, welcome the questions, root the faith. All of it is true and given by God, and none of it is the bottom. The bottom is a person and an act of trust. We entrust our children to God, because they were always more his than ours. The worried parent's case is strong: the stakes are eternal, so fear is appropriate, and a parent who isn't anxious about a child's soul doesn't love enough. There's love in that fear. But fear is a poor engine for raising a believer. It produces control and pressure, a home where faith feels like surveillance, the very thing that drives children away.

The gospel we want our children to believe is the gospel that frees us to parent them, because we aren't their savior; Christ is. "By grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God" (Ephesians 2:8). We sow in grace because we were saved by grace, and we hold our children with open hands because they were never ours to keep. Hannah said of the son she'd begged for, "I have lent him to the LORD" (1 Samuel 1:28). The study doesn't resolve, because no honest study of raising children can promise the ending. It points to the One who holds them.

keyScripture.why: "For this child I prayed, and the LORD has granted me my petition that I made to him. Therefore I have lent him to the LORD. As long as he lives, he is lent to the LORD" (1 Samuel 1:27-28). Hannah names the deepest act of a believing parent: entrusting a child back to the God who gave him, with open hands.

discussion.q: Every practice we've studied ends with something for you to do, but this session ends with entrusting your child to God. Why does it matter that the last word is an act of trust rather than a technique?
discussion.behind: Gather the whole study here. The practices are good, but they can become a performance and a burden. Move the room from doing to entrusting, from securing a child's faith to handing the child to the One who can give it. Let them feel the relief of an answer that's surrender, not effort.

discussion.q: Many of us parent from fear and call it love. Where can you find fear underneath your own parenting, and what does it tell you to do that grace wouldn't?
discussion.behind: This is the convicting center, so handle it with care. Most parents run on fear and have never named it. Fear produces control and pressure, and children feel it. Go first. Don't shame anyone; help the fear come into the light where grace can replace it.

discussion.q: The stakes really are eternal, so fear can feel appropriate, and yet fear is a poor engine for raising a believer. How do you hold both?
discussion.behind: Keep both halves. The stakes are eternal, and the leader mustn't minimize that. But fear produces the controlling, pressured home that drives children off. The answer to high stakes isn't fear but trust in the God who holds the stakes. That's the gospel applied to parenting.

discussion.q: Read Ephesians 2:8-9. How would your parenting change this week if you believed you're not your child's savior, and Christ is?
discussion.behind: Land on the gospel applied. Many parents functionally believe their effort saves their child, which is crushing and false. Help people feel the freedom of not being the savior, and the open hands that follow from grace. Invite specifics, and go first.

discussion.q: Looking back over all five sessions, what's the one thing about your child you most need to entrust to God tonight, and what has made it so hard to open your hands?
discussion.behind: Close the whole study by turning to ourselves and to the act of entrusting. Don't resolve it. Invite each person, the leader first, to name the child or the fear and why the hands stay closed. End with open hands held out toward God, not a tidy assurance.

objections.objection: The stakes are eternal. My child's soul hangs in the balance. So fear is appropriate, even loving. A parent who's calm about whether their child believes doesn't love the child enough.
objections.response: There's love in this. The stakes really are eternal, and a parent ought to care about a child's soul more than almost anything. The error isn't in caring. It's in believing fear is the right response to caring, and that fear produces faith. It doesn't. Fear in a parent produces control, because fear always grasps, and control produces a home where faith feels like pressure and surveillance, where God gets associated in a child's gut with anxiety and rules and the withdrawal of approval. A child raised that way often flees the faith precisely to escape the fear. The answer to eternal stakes isn't a parent who's calm because they don't care. It's a parent who has handed the eternal stakes to the God who actually holds them, and who therefore parents from rest instead of panic. You're right that the stakes are infinite. That's exactly why you can't carry them. Only God can, and the gospel is the news that he has.

objections.objection: If God is sovereign and only he gives faith, and there's no guarantee anyway, why does anything I do as a parent matter? This sounds like an excuse to stop trying.
objections.response: It's the opposite, and the distinction is everything. Entrusting your child to God isn't neglecting your child, any more than a farmer who trusts God for the harvest stops planting. We sow because we've been told to sow, and we sow in grace rather than fear because we ourselves were saved by grace and not by our performance. This session isn't saying do less. It's saying do the same things, the loving and teaching and answering and rooting, from a different engine: trust instead of terror, open hands instead of a white-knuckled grip. The parent who has entrusted a child to God often works more freely and patiently, because the weight of being the child's savior has been lifted and put where it belongs. You labor, and you entrust the outcome, and the entrusting keeps the labor from becoming the desperate, controlling thing fear makes it.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If you believed all the way down that God loves your child more than you do and can reach them anywhere, which child and which fear would you finally entrust to him tonight?
sessions.practice: This week, make the entrusting real, because it's easy to say and hard to do. Each day, take one child by name before God. Pray not a fearful prayer that grabs but a trusting one that releases: name the fear you carry for them, then place them in God's hands with words like, "This one is yours. You love them more than I do." When you catch yourself taking them back into your own grip of worry and control, open your hands again. At the end of the week, write down what it did to your fear, and to your parenting, to keep handing them over.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we've loved these children with everything we have, and we've parented them, more than we knew, from fear, gripping them as if their souls were ours to secure. We can't secure them. We aren't their savior. You are. Forgive the fear we called love and the control we called diligence. Free us to parent from grace, because we were saved by grace, to sow with open hands, and to love them without the panic that drives them away. And now we do the hardest thing. We give them back to you, the believing and the wandering alike, because they were always more yours than ours, and you love them more than we ever could, and you can reach them in any far country we can't follow them into. Hold our children, Lord. We entrust them to you. Amen.
reflection: What in my parenting is driven by fear that I've been calling love, and what would the same action look like if it came from grace?
Do I functionally believe I'm my child's savior, that my effort secures their soul, and what does that belief cost me and them?
Which of my children, and which fear, am I refusing to entrust to God, and what am I afraid would happen if I opened my hands?
sessions.teaching:
We've spent four sessions on things to do, and every one is true and given by God. Love God first, so your children can catch it. Talk about him in the ordinary, until faith is the air of your home. Welcome the hard questions, so your home is where doubt comes. Root the faith deep, so it survives the leaving. All good, all commanded. But if we stop there, we'll have turned raising believers into an exhausting performance, one more list of tasks to fail at, and the worried parent will add this study to everything else they aren't doing well enough to save their child. So we have to go underneath all of it. At the bottom isn't a method. It's a person and an act of trust. We don't finally save our children by parenting them well. We entrust them to the God who saves, because they were always more his than ours.

Start with the engine, because nearly everything in parenting runs on one of two fuels, and most of us are running on the wrong one without having named it. The fuels are fear and grace, and fear disguises itself as love so well that we usually can't tell them apart. We lie awake afraid for our children's souls and call it love. We control and hover and pressure and monitor and call it diligence. We tie our own peace to whether our children are walking with God this week and call it caring.

The worried parent's defense deserves a hearing, because most of us believe it. The stakes are eternal, he says. My child's soul hangs in the balance. How could fear not be appropriate? And the stakes really are eternal. A parent ought to care about a child's soul more than almost anything. The error isn't in the caring. It's in believing fear is the right response, and that fear produces faith. It doesn't. Fear in a parent produces control, because fear always grasps and tries to secure the outcome by force. Control produces a home where faith feels like pressure and surveillance and the constant threat of disappointing, where God is tied, in a child's gut, to anxiety and rules and the withdrawal of a parent's approval. And the child raised by fear very often flees the faith to flee the fear. The engine we trust most to keep our children believing is one of the surest ways to drive them off.

So what's the answer to eternal stakes? The gospel, applied to the parent first. Hand the eternal stakes to the God who holds them, and parent from rest instead of panic. You're right that the stakes are infinite. That's exactly why you can't carry them. A weight that size will crush any parent who tries to bear it, and it will crush the child underneath. Only God can carry the eternal weight of a child's soul, and the gospel we so want our children to believe is the news that Christ is the savior and we aren't.

The same gospel we want our children to believe frees us to parent them. "For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works" (Ephesians 2:8-9). We weren't saved by getting it right, and neither will our children be. So we can stop parenting as if our performance saves them. We can hold them with open hands, because they were never ours to keep, and love them without the frantic grip, because the grip was always an attempt to do God's job. And "he who began a good work" in a child is the one who "will bring it to completion" (Philippians 1:6), not us.

Then comes the hardest thing in the study, harder than the loving and teaching and rooting combined, the thing a believing parent has to do again and again for the rest of their life. We entrust our children to God. Think of Hannah, who prayed for a son with a desperation few of us have known, and who gave him back as soon as he was weaned. "For this child I prayed, and the LORD has granted me my petition that I made to him. Therefore I have lent him to the LORD" (1 Samuel 1:27-28). She held the most longed-for child in Israel with open hands. Think of the father in the parable, who didn't chase his son into the far country but watched the road, and "while he was still a long way off," saw him and ran (Luke 15:20). That father is the picture of entrusting: open hands that release a child into a country the parent can't follow them into, trusting the God who can. And hear what God says through Isaiah: "Can a woman forget her nursing child...? Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you. Behold, I have engraved you on the palms of my hands" (Isaiah 49:15-16). His love is more faithful than the best parent's.

Every parent who has gripped a child as though the grip were what kept them has to learn, and keep learning, that the grip is the problem, and that the most faithful thing a parent can do is what feels most like failure: open the hands and give the children back to the God who gave them, who loves them more than we can, and who can reach them where we can't.

So this study ends without a resolution, because no honest account of raising children can promise the ending, and a study that tied a bow on it would be lying to every parent of a prodigal in the room. It ends with a person and an act of trust. If you've been carrying the eternal weight of your child's soul as if it were yours to secure, put it down. You aren't the savior. Sow in grace. Parent from rest. Welcome the questions, root the faith, love God first in front of them, all of it, freely, with open hands. And give your children, the believing and the wandering alike, back to the One who made them and loves them and can hold them when they're far past everything you can reach.

scriptureStudy.note: "For this child I prayed... Therefore I have lent him to the LORD." Hannah gives back the very child she begged for, a picture of holding a longed-for child with open hands rather than a desperate grip.

"While he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran." The father entrusts and waits rather than chasing, and runs toward the son who returns, grace that releases and welcomes.

"For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works." The gospel that saved the parent by grace frees the parent to stop trying to save the child by works.

"Neither death nor life... nor things present nor things to come... will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord." Paul's confidence rests on God's love, not on our grip. That's the love a parent entrusts a child to.

"I am convinced that he is able to guard until that Day what has been entrusted to me." Paul entrusts what he can't keep to the One who can guard it, the very act a parent performs in handing a child to God.

"He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ." The work in a soul is God's, begun and completed by him, which frees a parent from believing the completion depends on their performance.

"Can a woman forget her nursing child...? Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you." God speaks to his people of a love more faithful than a mother's. That faithfulness is the ground on which a parent can let go.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, take up God's covenant promises and the prodigals together, because a believing parent lives between them and shouldn't resolve the tension falsely either way. On one side are the promises: the God "who keeps covenant and steadfast love with those who love him and keep his commandments, to a thousand generations" (Deuteronomy 7:9); Peter's word at Pentecost that "the promise is for you and for your children" (Acts 2:39); the long pattern of faith handed down in families, Lois to Eunice to Timothy. A parent should hold those promises, pray them, and lean on them. On the other side are the prodigals Scripture records without flinching: Esau, the sons of Samuel, the sons of David, and God's own lament over a people he raised who turned away: "Children have I reared and brought up, but they have rebelled against me" (Isaiah 1:2).

Christians read these promises differently. Some traditions see in them a covenant claim on the children of believers that shapes baptism and the hope a parent may hold; others read them as general patterns of grace with no promise attached to any particular child. Name both, and leave that question open. The errors on each side are cruel. Over-press the promise and you tell a prodigal's parent that the child's unbelief proves they failed, or that God broke his word. Over-press the prodigals and you rob a parent of real hope. Augustine's Confessions tells of his mother Monica praying for years for her wandering son; it's worth reading here. The deepest comfort isn't a guarantee about the child. It's the character of the God the child is given to.

leaderPrimer:
Every parent at this table carries the same fear, and nobody will name it in week one. The fear is that they're already failing, that the culture is stronger than their dinner table, that a clock is running out on their child's soul, and that this study exists to list everything they should have been doing all along. That's the danger in this room. A study on passing faith to children turns, almost by itself, into technique: five weeks of methods that quietly promise an outcome God never promised. The moment that happens, you've traded grace for formula, and every parent leaves more afraid than they came.

Guard against it from the first night, because almost certainly a parent in your group has a child who has already walked away. The father in session one did everything right and his daughter left anyway, and a father or mother like him is at your table wondering whether these five weeks will be a quiet accusation. Decide now that they won't be. Say plainly, early and more than once, that a child's wandering isn't a simple judgment on a parent's parenting, and that God parents people their own homes couldn't reach. When the group reaches the command to speak of God on the road and at the table (Deuteronomy 6), keep it an invitation to a shared life rather than a checklist to fail. The same passage can be either, depending on the tone of the person holding it.

Expect tears in session four, when parents imagine the leaving, and in session five, which asks them to open their hands. Rush no one. Keep the study's deepest claim in view: the goal was never to manufacture belief in a child, which no parent can do, but to live a faith worth inheriting and to trust the God who loves that child more than they do. Lead as a parent under the same grace, not as one whose children all turned out. Send them home lighter. Fear is what they carried in, and it would be a failure of all five weeks to send them out with more.

faq.q: Is this study going to make me feel guilty if my child has walked away from the faith?
faq.a: No, and it works hard to prevent that. The first session grants that Scripture lays the teaching of children on parents, and then refuses to let that become a club. The Bible records Isaac raising Esau, Samuel's sons taking bribes, and David weeping over a rebel son, which means faithful parenting can't guarantee a believing child without making those passages impossible. The study says again and again that a child's faith is finally God's gift, not the product of a parent's performance. If you came carrying grief over a child who has left, you'll find a study that sits in that grief with you, and a leader primer that tells the leader to say plainly that your child's wandering isn't a simple judgment on your parenting.

faq.q: Does this study think a child's faith is all up to the parents?
faq.a: No, and refusing to flatten that is the whole point. The home is the main place God hands on faith, the most important human soil there is, and a parent who hands it all to programs has missed what Deuteronomy commands. But the home isn't a machine that produces belief. Faithful sowing doesn't always yield the harvest a parent prayed for, because the new heart is God's gift, not something any household can manufacture. The study holds the home as decisive ground but not a deciding machine. You sow with everything you have and entrust the harvest to God.

faq.q: Is the study saying that if I follow the right method my children will believe?
faq.a: The opposite. The study says more than once, in plain words, that no method guarantees a believing child, because faith is God's gift and not the output of a technique. The leader primer warns that the greatest danger is letting the study become a method that promises results. The practices in it, loving God first, talking of him in the ordinary, welcoming questions, rooting the faith, are good and commanded, but they're sowing, not control. You sow because you're told to and because the home is the ground God most often uses, and then you entrust the outcome to him, the way a farmer plants in ground he can't finally command.

faq.q: If I raise my children right, are they guaranteed to keep the faith?
faq.a: Not guaranteed, and the study won't promise it. Proverbs says, "Train up a child in the way he should go; even when he is old he will not depart from it" (Proverbs 22:6), but that's a proverb, a general truth about how things usually go, not an iron promise, and reading it as a guarantee has crushed many faithful parents whose child wandered. The biblical hope is real. Faith is often handed down through generations, and a parent should pray God's promises and lean on them. But those promises sit beside the prodigals Scripture records without flinching. Faithful parenting is the ordinary ground God uses, not a guarantee of the harvest, and the study would rather tell you that than sell you a promise that leaves you blaming yourself if a child leaves.

faq.q: What do I do when my child asks a hard question I can't answer?
faq.a: Say, "I don't know that one. It's a hard question, and people who love God have wrestled with it. Let's look at it together," and stay confident in the God you do know. The study argues that faked certainty is the most fragile thing in the room, because it shatters the moment a child catches the bluff. A parent who shuts a question down teaches a child that the question is dangerous and that the parent can't be trusted with it, so the next doubt goes elsewhere or gets buried. You don't need to be a theologian. Deuteronomy gives parents not a philosophy but a story, what God has done, including in your own life. For the hard questions, your job is to be the trusted person who goes looking with your child.

faq.q: Should I protect my children from doubts and skeptics, or expose them?
faq.a: Neither extreme. Some sheltering of the young is right and good; a six-year-old doesn't need to debate atheists. But protection as the whole strategy, all the way to the door, produces a brittle, hothouse faith that has never met a real objection and gives way when the child leaves home. The aim is roots, not walls, a faith that knows not only what it believes but why. It's far better for a child to meet a first hard doubt at home with a loving parent at thirteen than alone at nineteen with a stranger eager to take it apart. So the wisdom is protection that gives way, over the growing years, to preparation, letting a child meet hard things gradually and with you.

faq.q: Why does the study keep talking about faith being caught more than taught?
faq.a: Because the Shema describes formation, not only information, and the modern home keeps reaching for the second. A child learns to pray the way they learn a mother tongue, by immersion long before understanding, living in a home where God is the air and the practices are simply done. The command to talk of God's words on the road and at the table comes after the command for the parent to love the Lord with all the heart, so the talk is meant to be the overflow of real love. A child can tell whether God is a parent's atmosphere or a topic a parent enforces. Information matters, and a child needs to know what they believe, but information without formation produces a child who can pass a doctrine quiz and has no love for God.

faq.q: What does the research on young adults leaving actually say?
faq.a: Kara Powell and Chap Clark's Sticky Faith (2011), drawing on research at Fuller Youth Institute, reported that young people whose faith lasted were often ones who'd had room to voice their hardest questions inside warm relationships before leaving home, while doubt forbidden and driven underground tended to go with a faith that looked fine until it gave way. The same work warned that a faith reduced to behavior management and rule-keeping, with the gospel missing, didn't hold. The deepest finding is a posture, not a program. The study uses this to confirm what Scripture already says, not to add a technique, and it's careful to say the research promises outcomes no more than Scripture does.

faq.q: I parent from fear. Is that wrong, given that the stakes really are eternal?
faq.a: The stakes are eternal, and the study grants that fully, but fear is still the wrong fuel. Fear in a parent produces control, because fear grasps, and control produces a home where faith feels like pressure and surveillance, where a child comes to associate God with anxiety and rules and the withdrawal of approval, and often flees the faith to flee the fear. The answer to eternal stakes isn't a parent who doesn't care. It's a parent who has handed the stakes to the God who actually holds them, and who therefore parents from rest. You're right that the stakes are infinite, and that's exactly why you can't carry them. Only God can, and the gospel is the news that he has.

faq.q: If God is sovereign and only he gives faith, why does my parenting matter at all?
faq.a: Entrusting your child to God isn't neglecting your child, any more than a farmer who trusts God for the harvest stops planting. We sow because we're commanded to, and we sow in grace rather than fear because we ourselves were saved by grace. The study isn't telling you to do less. It's telling you to do the same things, loving and teaching and answering and rooting, from a different engine: trust instead of terror, open hands instead of a white-knuckled grip. A parent who has entrusted a child to God often works more freely and patiently, because the weight of being the child's savior has been lifted. You labor, and you entrust the outcome, and the entrusting keeps the labor from becoming the controlling thing fear makes it.

faq.q: What does it actually mean to entrust my child to God?
faq.a: It means holding your child with open hands rather than a desperate grip, the way Hannah gave back the son she had begged for, saying, "Therefore I have lent him to the LORD" (1 Samuel 1:28). It's the daily act of bringing a child by name before God, naming the fear you carry for them, and placing them in his hands: this one is yours; you love them more than I do. The study admits this isn't once for all. We hand them over, take them back into our grip of worry, and have to open our hands again. It doesn't make the danger disappear or guarantee the outcome. It moves the weight onto the only One strong enough to carry it, the God who loves your child more than you do and can reach them in any far country you can't follow them into.

faq.q: Why does the study keep implicating the writer and the leader instead of just helping parents?
faq.a: Because you can't help an anxious or grieving parent from above without the help turning into either shame or distance. The study names the common failures plainly, prayers over beds not knowing whether they landed, a hard question answered badly, fear called diligence, a grip that thinks it keeps a child, and it doesn't exempt the writer or the leader. A leader who admits, "I can't save my children either," can sit beside other parents as a fellow struggler, which is where real comfort comes from. A study that pointed only at other people's parenting would let everyone perform and change no one.

faq.q: I'm a skeptic, or not sure what I believe. Is this study only for committed Christians?
faq.a: It tries to be worth your time even if you're unsure, because it refuses the cheap version of what you might expect. It doesn't promise that the right technique manufactures belief. It takes seriously that children walk away from even the most faithful homes, and it admits that the culture presses hard questions on the young that deserve real answers rather than slogans. It tells parents to engage doubt rather than shelter children from it, and to welcome questions rather than fear them. What it offers isn't a formula for producing believers but a claim that a person's deepest loves are formed at home, that this is worth taking seriously, and that the hope for any child rests finally on grace rather than a parent's performance. You can weigh that. The study doesn't ask you to pretend.

faq.q: How do I lead this if I have a child who has walked away from the faith?
faq.a: Your grief isn't a disqualification. It may be your greatest qualification. The study is built to be led by a fellow struggler, not someone whose children all turned out, and every discussion question has notes on what's behind it, and every session ends in prayer, so you won't be improvising. Your candor about your own grief, and about the truth that faithfulness doesn't guarantee outcomes, may be the most pastoral thing in the room, the permission that lets other grieving parents stop hiding. What you do need is to refuse to let the group blame any parent, yourself included, to keep the room safe for the wounded and the quietly grieving, to lift weight off parents rather than pile it on, and to point everyone, yourself first, to the God who loves these children more than any parent can.

timeline.event: Moses gives Israel the Shema, "Hear, O Israel," commanding parents to love the LORD with all their heart and then to teach his words to their children on the road and at the table, lying down and rising up.
Hannah, having begged God for a son, gives Samuel back to the LORD, "I have lent him to the LORD," Scripture's clearest picture of a parent entrusting a longed-for child to God.

The psalmists urge one generation to tell the next the glorious deeds of the LORD so the children will set their hope in God, Proverbs gathers wisdom on training a child, and the same era records David weeping over a rebel son.
Jesus welcomes the children brought to him, rebuking those who would keep them away, and tells of a father who watches the road and runs to his returning son.

Paul tells fathers not to provoke their children but to bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord, and reminds Timothy of the faith that dwelt first in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice.
Augustine's Confessions tells of his mother Monica, who prayed for years through his rebellion and unbelief, and became for the church the lasting example of a parent praying for a wandering child.
Martin Luther writes his catechisms, the Small Catechism for heads of households to teach the faith to their children at home.
The Westminster Assembly completes the Shorter Catechism, a question-and-answer summary of the faith widely used to teach children at home and in church.
Susanna Wesley raises her children with deliberate spiritual instruction, setting aside regular time with each one; two of her sons, John and Charles, go on to lead the Methodist revival.

Horace Bushnell publishes his Discourses on Christian Nurture (expanded as Christian Nurture, 1861), arguing that a child should grow up a Christian and never know himself otherwise, against a revivalism that expected only sudden conversion.

Age-graded schooling, programs, and youth ministry gradually move much of the forming of children's faith out of the home and into institutions, a great convenience that also quietly relieves parents of a duty Scripture laid on them.
The secularization of the West changes the conditions of belief, so faith becomes one contested option among many, and children are formed as much by a wider culture as by the home.
Kara Powell and Chap Clark publish Sticky Faith, reporting that young people whose faith lasted had often been given room to voice doubt in warm relationships before leaving home.

facilitatorScript.open:
Welcome, and thanks for being here. Our hopes and fears for our children are some of the hardest things to talk about in a room, so it takes courage to come. Before we start, three things. First, this is a safe room. You can say here that your child has walked away from God. You can say you don't know what you're doing. Nobody is going to blame you or hand you a technique to fix your family. Second, this study takes the home seriously, because the home really is where faith is most often handed on, and it also says plainly that no method guarantees a believing child, because faith is God's gift and faithful parents sometimes have prodigal children. We're not here to secure our children's souls by trying hard enough. Third, I'm inside this too. I can't save my children any more than you can save yours. We're not pointing at struggling parents from a safe distance. We are the struggling parents.

Tonight we're looking at ________. Let me read our key passage, and then we'll sit with it before we say anything else. There are no wrong answers in the first five minutes.
facilitatorScript.transition: We've looked hard at what the passage says. Now let's bring it home, into the week we're about to walk into, the ordinary hours with our children and the quiet ones after they're asleep, because that's where this either matters or it doesn't.
facilitatorScript.close: We're going to stop there, even though it isn't resolved, because raising children doesn't resolve on a schedule and pretending otherwise would be a lie. Take the weight of this to God this week rather than carrying your children alone. Try the practice. Sit with the reflection questions on your own. And if tonight stirred up grief over a child who has wandered, please hear that you are not being blamed in this room, and that the God who holds your child loves them more than you do. Let me pray for us before we go. Thank you for being in this room.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, set the ground rules about safety and blame, and walk slowly through session 1's opening questions. Say plainly that no method guarantees a believing child and that faithful parents sometimes have prodigals.
Week 2: Session 1, Whose Work Is This, full discussion and practice on loving God first and the limits of a parent's control.
Week 3: Session 2, On the Road and at the Table, with extended time on the Shema and faith as the air of the home rather than a scheduled slot.
Week 4: Session 3, When They Ask the Hard Things, part one, on welcoming questions and the cost of shutting them down.
Week 5: Session 3 continued, doubt as part of faith and the research on why young adults leave, with practice making home safe for hard questions.
Week 6: Session 4, A Faith That Survives Leaving, roots and walls, and preparing children for a world that doesn't believe.
Week 7: Session 5, Grace, Not Fear, and the Letting Go, the two engines of parenting and entrusting a child with open hands.
Week 8: Integration. Revisit the five practices, the Scripture index, and the child each parent is entrusting to God, with space for the grieving and for prayer over wandering children.

Week 4: Session 5, Grace, Not Fear, and the Letting Go, with a short closing, hands open toward the God who holds our children.

glossary.definition: The command of Deuteronomy 6, named for its first Hebrew word ("Hear"), calling parents to love the LORD with all their heart and then teach his words to their children in the ordinary rhythms of life. The backbone of how Scripture frames the handing on of faith.

The ordinary, repeated, often imperfect practice of a household reading Scripture, praying, and turning to God together. What forms a child is consistency and reality, not polish; a simple practice kept beats a grand one abandoned.

The shaping of a child's loves and habits by immersion and practice, the way a child learns a mother tongue, as distinct from information, the delivery of facts. Faith is caught more than taught, formed before it's explained, though both matter.

The deliberate teaching of the faith, often by question and answer. It complements formation, since a faith with no content collapses under the first hard question, and content without love is only a quiz passed.

A child who has wandered from the faith, from the parable of the son who took his inheritance into a far country. Faithful parents sometimes have prodigals, and a wandering child isn't a simple judgment on a parent.
A term from Kara Powell and Chap Clark's research for faith that lasts into adulthood, often found in young people given room to voice doubt in warm relationships before leaving home.

The Spirit's work of giving a person a new heart and faith, "born, not of blood nor of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man, but of God" (John 1:13). Because it's God's gift, no household can manufacture it, which both humbles and frees a parent.

The study's picture of the difference between sheltering a child from every challenge, which produces a brittle faith, and rooting a faith deep enough, the why under the what, to find water in a dry place after the child leaves home.

The unnamed engine of much parenting, in which a parent grips, controls, and pressures a child out of dread for their soul and calls it love. Fear produces the very atmosphere that drives children from the faith.

Parenting fueled by the gospel rather than dread, in which a parent who knows they aren't the savior loves, teaches, and roots their children with open hands, sowing because they were told to and entrusting the harvest to God.

The repeated act of handing a child back to God with open hands, as Hannah lent Samuel to the LORD, naming the fear and placing the child with the One who loves them more and can reach them where the parent can't.

God's promise to keep covenant "to a thousand generations" and his word that "the promise is for you and for your children." Christians read its reach differently. It's the ground of a parent's hope and prayer, held alongside the prodigals Scripture also records, a hope to lean on rather than a guarantee to claim.
A faith reduced to behavior management and rule-keeping, with God attached and the gospel missing. It doesn't hold, because once the rules no longer apply there's nothing in it worth keeping.

Charles Taylor's phrase for the modern condition in which belief has gone from the assumed background to one contested option among many, so that a young person loses faith less to a knockdown argument than to a world where unbelief simply feels more plausible.

promoKit.bulletinBlurb: Faith gets handed to children in two wrong ways: gripped so tightly that it becomes pressure, or shrugged off to the youth group. Almost no one stops to ask what God told parents to do. This five-session study works slowly through whose work a child's faith really is, the Shema's picture of faith woven into the ordinary home, answering hard questions instead of fearing them, a faith built to survive doubt and leaving home, and parenting from grace rather than fear. It takes the home seriously and refuses to sell parents a formula, because faithful parents sometimes have prodigals and the gospel, not technique, is the hope. Any tired parent can lead it with no preparation. Come as you are.
promoKit.pulpitAnnouncement: We're starting a five-week study on passing a lasting faith to our children, and before any parent braces, hear this. It won't hand you a formula and promise a believing child if you follow it. It takes the home seriously, because the home really is where faith is most often handed on, and it also says plainly that faithful parents sometimes have children who wander, and that the hope of any child is grace and not technique. No homework, and no preparation needed to lead a group. If you carry hopes or fears for your children, this is for you. Sign up at the welcome table.
promoKit.inviteCaption: God answered the question of how to hand faith to the next generation by telling parents to love him first and then talk about him on the road and at the table. A five-session study on raising believers in a world that doesn't believe. It takes the home seriously, refuses to promise a formula, and is honest that faithful parents sometimes have prodigals. Come as you are.
quoteCards: The home is the ground God most often uses to hand on faith. It isn't a machine that produces it.
You can't hand on what you don't hold. Deuteronomy tells the parent to love God first, and only then to teach the child.
A child can tell whether God is the air a parent breathes or a topic a parent enforces.
The home that raises a durable faith isn't the one with all the answers. It's the one where any question is safe.
Better a first hard doubt at home with you at thirteen than alone at nineteen with a stranger eager to take it apart.
You can't fireproof a child. You can give them roots deep enough to find water in a dry place.
Fear is a poor engine for raising a believer.
You aren't your child's savior. Christ is, and that's the news that frees you to parent with open hands.
